title: Householder Motion Embedding: Noise Modulation for Motion-Controllable Video Generation
claim: Prior methods warp noise spatially and need costly correction; ours transforms noise per location by construction, enabling several control tasks.
layout: Top two side-by-side panels (a)/(b), bottom row of three application panels
description: The figure has two rows. The top row is split by a vertical line into (a) Prior: Spatial Noise Warping and (b) Ours: Householder Motion Embedding. In (a), a grayscale pixel grid with orange highlighted cells and orange arrows (a deformation field) goes through a 'White Noise Transport' arrow to a coarse 3x3 grayscale grid labelled Temporally Correlated Noise. In (b), a 3x3 grid of cells, each holding a star of black vectors for per-location Householder orthogonal transformations, goes through a 'Per-location Transform' arrow to a similar 3x3 grayscale grid. The bottom row has three panels: (c1) Motion Transfer, with an astronaut and a reference video of a walking person; (c2) Local Object Motion Control, with a penguin, a motion-signal mask and a red arrow; (c3) Camera Motion Control, with an aerial view of a castle, a 3D camera trajectory and film-strip outputs. Purple arrows lead to the film-strip outputs.
caption: We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), a simple noise-modulation method for motion-controllable diffusion video generation. (a) Prior methods rely on spatial noise warping driven by motion fields. They preserve spatial Gaussianity only through costly correction steps. (b) HME instead applies per-location Householder transformations in channel space to the noise. It preserves spatial Gaussianity by construction, with a 2.7× speed-up and better motion adherence. HME naturally supports (c1) motion transfer, (c2) local object motion control, and (c3) camera motion control.
abstract: Diffusion models for video generation have achieved remarkable success, yet precise motion control under explicit user guidance remains challenging. Recent noise-warping methods introduce temporal correlations by warping the noise according to the user-provided motion signal. However, standard spatial warping generally disrupts the noise's i.i.d. Gaussian structure, requiring distribution correction, such as Jacobian-based correction, but at a substantial computational overhead. We propose Householder Motion Embedding (HME), which encodes the motion signal into the noise through a sequence of Householder reflections that together form an orthogonal transformation applied to each location's channel vector. HME exactly preserves the spatial Gaussian structure within each frame while introducing cross-frame correlations that promote temporally consistent video. HME is agnostic to the network architecture and integrates directly into standard video diffusion fine-tuning pipelines. Experiments on different scenarios show that HME matches or outperforms the state of the art, while achieving a 2.7x speedup over noise warping. These results demonstrate that channel-space Householder transformations offer a principled and efficient alternative to noise warping for motion-controllable video generation.
